classification.difficultyReason: Proves chord-product results for four regular polygons, using exact ratios and the preceding pentagon result.

content.prompt: Consider the figures shown below. These depict an equilateral triangle, a square, a regular pentagon and a regular hexagon, and each is inscribed in a circle of radius 1.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
The vertices $A$, $B$ and $C$ of an equilateral triangle lie on a circle of radius 1. Show that
$$AB\times AC=3.$$

spec.description: Equilateral triangle inscribed in a circle; the two chords from A are highlighted.
spec.mathematics: Circle radius 1; vertices A, B, C in clockwise order, separated by central angles of 120 degrees.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied geometry and vertex labels are visible.

answer.short:
$AB=AC=\sqrt3$, so $AB\times AC=3$.

Bisect a central triangle and use $\sin60^\circ$.
answer.worked:
Join the centre $O$ to $A$ and $B$. Then $\angle AOB=120^\circ$. The perpendicular from $O$ to $AB$ bisects both the chord and this angle. Since the radius is 1,
$$\begin{align*}AB&=2\sin60^\circ\\AB&=2\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)\\AB&=\sqrt3.\end{align*}$$
The equilateral triangle has $AC=AB$. Thus
$$AB\times AC=\sqrt3\times\sqrt3=3.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt:
The vertices $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ of a square lie on a circle of radius 1. Show that
$$AB\times AC\times AD=4.$$

spec.description: Inscribed square with highlighted AB and AD, and separately highlighted diameter AC.
spec.mathematics: Circle radius 1; consecutive vertices separated by central angles of 90 degrees; AC is a diameter.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied geometry and vertex labels are visible.

answer.worked:
$AC$ is a diameter, so $AC=2$. Triangle $ABC$ is a $45^\circ$–$45^\circ$–$90^\circ$ triangle. Hence
$$\begin{align*}AB&=2\sin45^\circ\\AB&=\sqrt2.\end{align*}$$
The square has $AD=AB$. Therefore
$$AB\times AC\times AD=\sqrt2\times2\times\sqrt2=4.$$

Hint: You may refer to exercise 6.

spec.description: Regular inscribed pentagon with all four chords from A highlighted.
spec.mathematics: Circle radius 1; consecutive vertices separated by central angles of 72 degrees; diagonals AC and AD are supplied.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied geometry and vertex labels are visible.

answer.short:
$AB\times AC\times AD\times AE=5$.

Use the exact values from exercise 6 to obtain $AB^2=\frac{(5-\sqrt5)}{2}$ and $AC^2=\frac{(5+\sqrt5)}{2}$.
answer.worked:
The central angles for $AB$ and $AC$ are $72^\circ$ and $144^\circ$. Bisecting the corresponding isosceles triangles gives $AB=2\sin36^\circ$ and $AC=2\sin72^\circ$. Using exercise 6,
$$AB=AE=\sqrt{\frac{5-\sqrt5}{2}},\qquad AC=AD=\sqrt{\frac{5+\sqrt5}{2}}.$$
Thus
$$\begin{align*}AB\times AC\times AD\times AE&=AB^2AC^2\\AB\times AC\times AD\times AE&=\frac{5-\sqrt5}{2}\cdot\frac{5+\sqrt5}{2}\\AB\times AC\times AD\times AE&=\frac{25-5}{4}\\AB\times AC\times AD\times AE&=5.\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: of a regular hexagon lie on a circle of radius 1. Show that
The results obtained in this exercise can be generalised to a regular
-gon, but we will not do this here.

spec.description: Regular inscribed hexagon with chords from A highlighted; diameter AD has a distinct accent.
spec.mathematics: Circle radius 1; consecutive vertices separated by central angles of 60 degrees; diagonals AC, AD and AE are supplied.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied geometry and vertex labels are visible.

answer.worked:
Each central angle between consecutive vertices is $60^\circ$, so the triangles formed by two adjacent radii are equilateral. Hence $AB=AF=1$. Also, $AD$ is a diameter, so $AD=2$. Bisecting the $120^\circ$ central triangle gives
$$\begin{align*}AC&=2\sin60^\circ\\AC&=\sqrt3.\end{align*}$$
By symmetry, $AE=AC$. Therefore
$$AB\times AC\times AD\times AE\times AF=1\times\sqrt3\times2\times\sqrt3\times1=6.$$
